Sharded subscriber-vector fan-out with per-subscriber channel handoff and a slow-receiver phase; a withdrawing subscriber releases a Send that is waiting for it.
Single distributor relays to private one-value channels: lossless and ordered, one value of slack per subscriber, a stalled subscriber stalls the publisher.

DropOldest per-subscriber channels supply a nonblocking latest-oriented broadcast. Each slot carries a delivery lease (repair), so a subscriber may leave, and the caster may close, while a Send is in progress. The adapter selects the DropOldest policy; a handle is a pointer into the slab and must be closed exactly once, which the adapter ensures.
Lossy bounded ring reports overwrite counts and supports independent subscriber cursors; this adapter consumes lag notifications and is covered by direct accounting tests.
Immutable sequence-stamped ring nodes allow stateless independent cursors; overrun is counted and SendBatch coalesces wakeups.

Preallocated page slots plus a shared pong barrier provide acknowledged synchronous fan-out. Unsubscribe takes and acknowledges a value that an in-flight Send hands the departing subscriber (repair), so a subscriber may leave during a round. The API requires one Wait for every receive; the adapter acknowledges each value before it returns it.
Bounded Disruptor-style ring uses independent subscriber cursors and explicit Missed accounting; each publication coalesces wake signals.
Power-of-two sequence ring with independent cursors; Publish blocks at capacity until every attached cursor advances, preserving each value in order.
Independent cursor attach/detach supports changing subscriber membership while publication continues; each new cursor begins at the current head.
Context-bound cursor iterators detach on cancellation, and Close wakes receivers while allowing already-published values to drain.
With no cursors, publication is immediately available; later cursors start at the current head and observe subsequent values only.
Response 47's atomic-state caster plus pong barrier sends once to each registered receiver and waits for each receive acknowledgement.
Context iterators register synchronously and withdraw between publication rounds; Send includes the current subscriber set.
Send returns immediately with no subscribers and later subscriptions participate in later sends.

Generation-tracked latest value coalesces intermediates; a closed generation channel wakes all current observers and Load returns a coherent snapshot.
Observers are per-cursor generation snapshots with no registration in the publisher; churn does not mutate fan-out state.
Send is independent of observer count; each observer begins at the current generation and observes later updates only.
The response-51 extension preserves synchronous receive acknowledgements for live subscribers while retaining a bounded history for late joins.
Two phase-alternating unbuffered transports carry cooperative relays; Send waits for all receipt/relay handoffs, but not for application processing after Received.
Every subscriber in the membership snapshot receives each value before Send returns; Close of an outstanding subscription releases its share without counting delivery.
Membership is a locked count rather than a subscriber registry; independent subscription cursors can join or close around publication snapshots.
Send with no registered subscriptions returns zero without allocating an epoch; later subscriptions participate only in later sends.

Context-aware Recv and idempotent caster Close wake parked readers, allow retained values to drain, then return ErrRingClosed.
Each subscription has an independent bounded channel; publications are lossless in order and a full queue backpressures Send until read or per-subscription Close.
The one-element queue can accept a value before the subscriber reads it, so this is explicitly not a receive barrier; attached as a measured mismatch.
Correct exact delivery, but Send walks and synchronously enqueues to every cursor; this is a deliberate poor-fit measurement for O(1) high fan-out.
Membership uses immutable copy-on-write snapshots; churn performs O(N) copy work but never mutates a snapshot being traversed by Send.

O(1)-with-fanout sequence ring retains bounded history; each Next reports exact overwritten publications while Publish only replaces one shared generation signal.
Publication does not sweep subscriber state; a shared generation notification wakes independently paced cursors, with scheduling work paid by actual awakened readers.
Subscriptions own independent cursors and Done channels; attach/detach does not mutate publication fan-out work.
Unsubscribe is idempotent and signals Done; Close wakes selectors, permits retained values to drain, then reports closed.
With no active cursors Publish advances sequence without copying; later subscriptions start at the next publication and cannot read stale ring slots.
Atomic replay-snapshot plus live registration yields the retained suffix without a gap or duplicate; capacity is fixed and older history is intentionally unavailable.
Textbook mutex-protected bounded history plus per-subscriber buffered channels; snapshot and registration share one lock, with send backpressure on slow readers.
Mutex-protected per-subscriber bounded queues provide ordinary lossless backpressure; replay history is an additional bounded retention cost.
Subscriber registration and removal participate in the replay/send lock protocol; live readers withdraw by compensating the active one-shot send count.
Send retains history while no live subscribers exist; the harness adapter intentionally uses live-only Subscribe, then tests future delivery.

Closed notification epochs wake all waiters; a sequence-stamped bounded ring lets observers catch up and eventually see the latest value without blocking publishers.
No central subscriber registry; each iterator keeps an independent sequence cursor and can be cancelled independently.
Publication does not require registered observers; new iterators begin at the generation captured when SubscribeContext is called.

Ordinary mutex plus private unbounded slice queues and a coalescing wake channel; sender never waits for a consumer.

Membership edits copy a snapshot rather than locking the publish traversal; per-subscriber leases make withdrawal safe.

A lagging cursor can skip to the retained window and eventually observe the newest value; publication never waits for readers.

Overwritable seqlock ring with independent cursors; overwritten values are reported as dropped counts per cursor (TryRead/ReadContext). Attached ahead of 59's combiner front-end.

Atomic packed value+revision word; watch semantics by re-reading the word. No wake primitive exists by design (the candidate is a non-parking polling register), so the adapter supplies one on the test side: Publish posts to a wake gate after the word swap and Receive parks on it. The measured publish cost therefore includes one non-blocking channel send that is the adapter's, not the candidate's; conflation is the whole point of the cell.
Latest-value cell with version-gated WaitFor wakeups; watchers coalesce arbitrarily many sets into one read. Exactly the conflating-watch envelope.

Latest-value cell with coalesced generation-gated wakeups; this adapter tail-attaches by a subscribe-time epoch anchor and blocks on the cell's condvar-gated Watch path (no polling). Delivery is conflated under load: only the newest pending value is retained.

SPSC seqlock telemetry ring; publishers overwrite the oldest entry and readers observe seqlock-validated values with lag detectable via advertised head. Parked readers wake through an armed-waiter count and a relayed token (completion-phase repair: the single shared token used to wake one reader of many). Not attachable to zero-subscriber facets (no published-count accessor); single publisher only, so the concurrent test drivers serialise publishes for this adapter.
Epoch-gated seqlock broadcast ring with self-serve cursors; lapped cursors skip to the oldest retained value and report Skip counts (the scenario's detectable-loss criterion).
Bounded ring with per-subscription skip accounting (Subscription65Deepseek.Skipped); overwritten generations are counted, never delivered torn.
Bounded horizon ring; lapped readers recover per CatchUpPolicy (SkipToOldest attached) with capability status reporting and lag accounting.
Bounded ring with per-cursor lap detection; Next reports the exact number of overwritten tickets (skipped) with each return.
Bounded ring with per-cursor skip accounting (Lag/Missed) and lossless ordered delivery while the cursor keeps up.
Stateless cursors; subscription churn never mutates ring state.
Subscription is a stateless ring cursor; publish-side combining lanes are unaffected by subscriber churn.
Watchers are stateless; attach/detach is a free read of the atomic word.
Watchers register only while parked in WaitFor; churn costs one wait-free slot per active waiter.
Watchers are stateless cursors over an epoch counter; churn never mutates publisher state.
Readers are independent cursors over the ring; no membership registry exists, so joining and leaving cost nothing.
Watchers hold private cursors; no registry, no fan-out state.
Subscriptions are independent cursors; churn does not touch the publish path.
Stateless cursors; subscription churn never mutates ring state.
Cursors are caller-owned values; attach/detach is local to each session.
Cursors are caller-owned with no publisher-side registry.
Publish with no cursors is one slot claim plus a fenced write.
Submit with no cursors still completes synchronously through the combining lanes.
Publish with no watchers is a single atomic word swap.
Publish with no watchers is an atomic store and a no-op broadcast.
Publish with no watchers is a store plus an O(1) wake broadcast.
Publish with no readers is two seqlock stores, a slot write, a head store and one non-blocking notifier send. A late reader attaches at Head()+1.
Publish with no watchers arms no gate; one claim CAS and a fenced slot write.
Publish with no subscriptions writes the slot and advances head.
Publish with no readers is one sequence claim and a slot write.
Publish with no cursors is a striped CAS and a slot store.
Publish with no cursors is one slot-claim CAS and a fenced write.
ReadContext returns on ctx cancellation; Close is idempotent and wakes parked readers.
ReadContext honours ctx; adapter Close closes the backing ring (Combiner itself has no separate Close).
Receive exits on ctx cancellation; Close flips the closed bit in the same packed word.
WaitFor returns on cancellation or close; Close is idempotent.
Watch iterators end on ctx cancellation; Close is idempotent and wakes parked watchers.
Receive exits on ctx cancellation; no global Close exists by design (the notifier never closes), so adapter Close is a no-op.

Receive blocks in NextContext (added in the completion phase next to the candidate's Next: the same wait, plus the caller's context); Close is idempotent.
ReadNext returns on ctx; Close is idempotent and wakes parked readers.
Next returns on ctx; Close releases parked cursors.
WaitNextContext returns on ctx; Close wakes every parked waiter; idempotent.
Publish is one sequence claim plus a fenced slot write regardless of cursor count.
Publish amortizes combining cost under contention; fan-out cost stays O(1) for the write path.
Publish is a single atomic word swap regardless of watcher count.
Publish is one atomic store plus an O(1) wake broadcast regardless of waiter count.
Publish is one store plus an O(1) generation flip regardless of watcher count.
Publish is one claim CAS plus a fenced write regardless of watcher count; no per-watcher work.

Publish is one striped CAS plus a slot store regardless of cursor count.
Publish is one slot-claim CAS plus a fenced write regardless of cursor count.

Single-publisher seqlock ring of plain-data values stored as whole 64-byte lines; cursors are caller-owned and every read reports the exact number of positions skipped. Overlapping Publish calls panic by contract; the concurrent test drivers serialise publishes for this adapter (measurements publish from one goroutine and are unaffected).
Cursors are plain values with no registry: attach/detach costs nothing on the publish path.
Publish with no cursors is two stamped stores and a head store; Subscribe tail-attaches so a late cursor sees only later values.
Next returns on ctx; Close is idempotent, unparks every cursor and leaves committed entries readable.
Publish cost is independent of cursor count; wake is skipped entirely when no cursor is parked.

Multi-sender ring with a one-word reader/writer pin per slot; a lapped cursor skips forward and the loss is visible as sequence gaps and in Lost(). Parked cursors are woken by a counted token cascade on one shared unbuffered channel: the sender sends one token and the receivers forward the rest as a binary tree.
A cursor is a position with no registry: subscribe and unsubscribe write no shared state and allocate nothing.
Send with nothing armed is a mutex round-trip, two slot-lock adds, a tail store and one atomic load; Cursor tail-attaches.

Recv disarms on ctx (taking and forwarding its wake token if a round already claimed it); Close wakes every parked cursor and retained values stay readable. Send after Close panics by design; the adapter checks Closed() first.
The sender's wake cost is one channel send regardless of the number of parked cursors; the remaining N-1 sends are performed by the woken subscribers.

Per-subscriber unbuffered channels driven from a slot arena: Broadcast returns after one rendezvous per subscriber (try-send, bounded spin, then park). Fixed subscriber capacity chosen at construction (adapter: 1024 slots).
Unsubscribe during an in-flight send hands the slot over through a drain protocol so the broadcaster is never stalled by a departing subscriber; slots are generation-tagged against reuse.
Receivers select on the caster's Done channel; Close waits for, and does not interrupt, a broadcast already in flight (by design).
Broadcast with no subscribers is a turnstile round-trip and one coordination CAS.
Delivery is one sequential rendezvous per subscriber: cost grows linearly with fan-out and every subscriber waits for those ahead of it. Attached to document the mismatch.

BroadcastPhased delivers to every subscriber and then waits for each to Ack or Unsubscribe; the adapter acknowledges immediately after receipt. The separate acknowledgement and the sender deadline are exercised in deadline-bounded-barrier-broadcast.
Same lifecycle as the 1-phase mode; Close during the acknowledgement wait makes BroadcastPhased return an error (integration repair).

Epoch-published value plus an explicit pending-acknowledgement count; Broadcast returns when every member joined at publish time has acked the epoch or left. One barrier channel is allocated per broadcast.
Join and Leave take the same mutex as Broadcast's publish step; Leave decrements the pending count for an unacked member so churn cannot stall the publisher.
Wait returns on ctx; Close releases every waiter and an in-flight Broadcast, which reports the closure (integration repair).
Broadcast with no members publishes the epoch and returns without allocating a barrier.

Publish notifies members with one non-blocking send each under the cohort mutex, and every acknowledgement takes that same mutex: correct at any size, but the barrier serialises all members. Attached to document the mismatch.
Per-subscriber single-slot mailbox with offer and acknowledgement epochs; Send returns once every subscriber has read the value (reading is the acknowledgement) or closed.
The subscriber list is copy-on-write; a subscriber closing mid-send wakes the waiting sender.
Next returns on ctx; Close closes every subscriber, releasing an in-flight Send (which then reports success: a closed subscriber counts as departed).
Send with no subscribers is a mutex round-trip and an epoch increment.
Offers are posted to all subscribers before any acknowledgement is awaited, so subscribers proceed in parallel, but the sender still performs O(N) offers and waits. Attached to document the mismatch.

attachments.exposure: Exposure limited: no concurrent receiver withdrawal or cancellation during a Send/Wait round; the response counts acknowledgements globally and cannot reclaim a missing acknowledgement, so no churn/abandonment facet may run.
attachments.remarks: Shared ChanCaster channel with a condition-variable pong barrier; the registered receive count is acknowledged before Send returns.
The reference dual-counter rendezvous protocol with cache-line isolation and RecvContext/TryRecv helpers; withdrawal still compensates an active Send.
Atomic packed-state one-shot receiver accounting; Add and Send coordinate through CAS and a parked positive-add barrier.
Single-channel scatter with steal compensation on last withdrawal: the novel design under test.
Condvar ring admits without waiting, evicts the oldest pending item at capacity and counts eviction; one shared cursor dispatches to one waiter.
Ordinary buffered channel with serialized make-room-then-enqueue admission; no novel ring or wakeup machinery.

Explicit poor-fit comparison: the condvar ring admits before a worker receives and can evict under overload, so it does not provide the lossless receipt-coupled scatter invariant; its good-fit scenario is bounded-competing-consumer-overflow.
Vacuum baseline: an ordinary unbuffered channel already dispatches to exactly one ready receiver.
Dual of the reference caster: Wait receives once per sender, Add(-1) compensates.
Vacuum baseline: mutex-guarded count + one unbuffered channel + compensating sends.
Vacuum async baseline (BaselineFanout) carrying multi-word payloads.
Atomic slot publication: payload is observed via a single pointer/word swap.
Ring slot publication for wide payloads.
Shared ring carrying wide payloads by value.
Ring feed carrying wide payloads (drop-oldest).
Ring feed carrying wide payloads (blocking/lossless mode).

Seqlock ring: wide-payload torn-read risk is exactly what this scenario probes.

Per-producer bounded SPSC lanes with an MPSC ready-stack and amortised batch drain; drop-newest with push-time accounting (TryPush false / TryPushBatch short count); FIFO per lane, no global ordering; Close drains accepted values before reporting closure. The scenario's intended design.

Vacuum baseline: one shared buffered channel behind one mutex (push path), select-default drops counted in Drops(); single lock domain, no lane isolation or batching — the ordinary design the port must beat.

Slot arena (default 32 slots): a caller first tries to claim a waiting offer, otherwise publishes its own in a free slot, rescans for a concurrent offer, spins briefly and parks on the slot's wake channel; cancellation rolls the offer back with one CAS or completes the match if it lost the race.

The same exchanger with a one-slot arena: no elimination spread, every caller contends on one state word. Attached to expose the arena's contribution and the rescan/withdraw paths under maximum collision.
Vacuum baseline: one mutex, one waiting-offer pointer, a buffered reply channel allocated per parked offer; cancellation withdraws under the lock.

BroadcastPhased(ctx): sequential rendezvous delivery, then a wait for every Ack; a deadline during the acknowledgement wait marks each unacknowledged slot as owing one late Ack, which is absorbed. A second consecutive abandoned broadcast to the same unacknowledging subscriber is outside what the marker can represent (recorded limit; the facets acknowledge every received value before receiving again).

Broadcast(ctx): the value is published under an epoch and the publisher waits on a pending-acknowledgement count; a deadline abandons the barrier (the value stays published), acknowledgements carry their epoch so a late one is ignored, and Leave compensates. A member that missed an abandoned value is handed the latest one.

Send(ctx): reading is the acknowledgement, so there is no separate barrier step and no late acknowledgement to tolerate; a deadline leaves the value in each unread mailbox to be overwritten by the next Send.

Vacuum baseline: per-member unbuffered channel, a fresh one-slot acknowledgement channel per member per send, and a select on the sender's context and the member's departure at every blocking point. Allocates per member per send.

invariants: every subscriber receives every value exactly once, in publish order
Send does not return before every subscriber registered at send time has received (and, where the API separates it, acknowledged)
no delivery to subscribers registered after the send
scenarios.title: Lock-step lossless broadcast with acknowledgement barrier
scenarios.tradeoffs: Publisher latency is bounded by the slowest subscriber; throughput does not scale with fan-out, in exchange for a hard delivery+ack guarantee and in-order delivery.
scenarios.use_case: Ordered command/config distribution for consumers that must all receive and acknowledge each value before the publisher may proceed

invariants: each Send is received by exactly the receivers registered for that round
Send's return equals the number of actual receives
a withdrawing receiver can never hang a Send
scenarios.title: Rendezvous cast to N receivers without post-receive barrier
scenarios.tradeoffs: Send performs one rendezvous per receiver and returns at receipt, not after processing; cheapest possible synchronous fan-out, but receivers must re-register per round and a missing receiver stalls the sender.
scenarios.use_case: Synchronous hand-off of each value to a known set of receivers for lock-step simulation ticks and staged pipelines where receipt itself is the synchronisation

invariants: every subscriber receives every value in order
Send returns after handoff to all subscribers registered at send time
scenarios.title: Synchronous handoff broadcast without acknowledgement barrier
scenarios.tradeoffs: Send waits for handoff (receipt/readiness) but not processing; faster than a full barrier and still lossless, but a subscriber that never becomes ready stalls the publisher.
scenarios.use_case: Tick/phase distribution for workers that must all be handed the current value before it is superseded, where processing acknowledgement is unnecessary

invariants: while subscribers keep lag below capacity, every value is delivered in order
Send applies backpressure instead of dropping
memory stays bounded regardless of publish volume
scenarios.title: Buffered lossless broadcast with backpressure
scenarios.tradeoffs: Memory is bounded by per-subscriber capacity; publisher can be stalled by the slowest consumer (or must use a context/try variant); delivery stays lossless and ordered while lag < capacity.
scenarios.use_case: Event streaming for consumers with independent pacing and bounded lag tolerance, where no event may be lost and a lagging consumer should slow the publisher rather than drop data

invariants: received values are strictly increasing (no duplicates, no reordering, no torn values)
the final value is always eventually observable
Send never blocks on a slow consumer
scenarios.title: Bounded ring broadcast, lossy under overrun with detectable skips
scenarios.tradeoffs: Send is O(1)-ish and never waits for consumers; consumers that fall more than capacity behind lose values, but the loss is reported (skipped/missed) so they can resync.
scenarios.use_case: High-rate telemetry/market-data style feeds for many consumers where keeping up matters more than completeness and a consumer must be able to tell (and count) what it missed

invariants: observed values are strictly increasing and the latest published value is always eventually observed
Send never blocks on any subscriber
no stale value is observed after a newer one
scenarios.title: Latest-value conflating broadcast / watch
scenarios.tradeoffs: Intermediate values may be conflated away entirely; in exchange Send is non-blocking, cheap at any fan-out, and watchers can never be stalled by (or stall) the publisher.
scenarios.use_case: State observation — configuration snapshots, health/progress, cache invalidation — for watchers that only ever care about the newest state and integrate with select

invariants: every subscriber can eventually read every value published after it subscribed, in order, however far behind it falls
scenarios.title: Unbounded catch-up broadcast (full history replay)
scenarios.tradeoffs: Delivery is lossless for arbitrarily lagging consumers; in exchange memory retention is pinned by the slowest live consumer and grows without bound if one never reads.
scenarios.use_case: Audit/event-sourcing style distribution for late or slow consumers that must eventually see every value in order, where retention cost is accepted

invariants: a joining observer sees the retained suffix in order with no gap or duplicate at the live boundary
all values published after registration are delivered once in order
retention is bounded by configured capacity and older history is intentionally absent
scenarios.title: Bounded recent-history catch-up with lossless live delivery
scenarios.tradeoffs: Memory remains bounded and a new observer can replay the recent window atomically with live registration; a larger window costs more snapshot/copy work and cannot satisfy full audit-history requirements.
scenarios.use_case: Late observers need a recent context window before joining a live, ordered stream, and deliberately accept that history older than a fixed retention bound is unavailable

invariants: every active subscription receives every accepted value exactly once in FIFO order
Send does not wait for consumer readiness
a slow consumer's backlog does not reorder or block another consumer
withdrawal stops future admission without losing already accepted backlog
scenarios.title: Nonblocking lossless fan-out with private unbounded overflow
scenarios.tradeoffs: Slow consumers are isolated in private FIFO queues and cannot apply backpressure or cause loss; retained memory grows with lag and can exhaust the process, unlike bounded rings or backpressured buffers.
scenarios.use_case: Event notification where a publisher must never wait for any consumer and every active consumer must eventually receive every value, accepting per-consumer memory growth as the price

invariants: every dispatched value is received by exactly one receiver
Send returns 0 iff no receiver was registered, 1 iff exactly one received (including via steal compensation)
withdrawal of the last receiver never hangs a Send
scenarios.title: Work distribution to exactly one receiver (scatter / competing consumers)
scenarios.tradeoffs: No broadcast cost and natural load balancing (whichever worker is ready wins); in exchange delivery is exactly-one, so this is useless for notification, and a withdrawing worker must never orphan an in-flight dispatch.
scenarios.use_case: Task dispatch for a dynamic worker pool where each item must be processed by exactly one worker and workers join/leave freely

invariants: Send never blocks on subscriber readiness
input and dispatch eviction are separately counted
each subscriber observes retained values in increasing order without duplicates
the final value of a burst is eventually observable after overload clears
scenarios.title: Bounded asynchronous fan-out dispatch with detectable overload
scenarios.tradeoffs: A central input queue absorbs bursts and decouples publication from fan-out, but adds dispatch latency and a second loss stage; pooled channels bound allocation while slow subscribers lose oldest mail with observable counters.
scenarios.use_case: Bursty event publication where the publisher should enqueue quickly and a dispatcher fans out to independent subscriber mailboxes, accepting bounded loss when either stage overloads

invariants: each retained value is received by at most one worker
accepted values that are not evicted are received exactly once in FIFO order
admission never blocks on worker readiness
overwrite-oldest eviction increments an exact dropped count
scenarios.title: Bounded competing-consumer dispatch with explicit overload eviction
scenarios.tradeoffs: Unlike rendezvous scatter, admission does not wait for a worker; unlike lossless work distribution, a full queue evicts pending work. The drop counter makes overload visible and the retained suffix remains FIFO.
scenarios.use_case: Work queues where admission must remain nonblocking and memory must stay bounded, but each accepted item is processed by exactly one worker and overload may evict the oldest pending item with an observable counter

invariants: Wait returns after exactly one signal per registered sender
a withdrawing sender is compensated so Wait cannot hang
Wait's return equals the number of real (non-compensated) signals
scenarios.title: Signal gathering from N senders (N-to-1 barrier)
scenarios.tradeoffs: Wait performs one rendezvous per registered sender; a sender that withdraws without signalling must be compensated or Wait hangs, which is the central correctness hazard of the family.
scenarios.use_case: Phase/completion barriers for a dynamic set of producers whose signals must all be collected before a coordinator proceeds (the dual of casting)

invariants: every accepted value is observed by the consumer exactly once, in per-producer FIFO order
TryPush/TryPushBatch report refusal (false/short count) exactly when the value was not accepted — loss is observable at push time
total buffered values never exceed the sum of lane capacities
after Close returns, all accepted values are drainable and Next eventually reports closure
scenarios.title: Bounded fan-in merge (M producers, one batch-oriented consumer)
scenarios.tradeoffs: The consumer is a single serialization point, unlike broadcast; producers must never block behind a slow consumer, so each lane is bounded and drops newest values at push time (counted at push), trading completeness for liveness and bounded memory. Ordering is FIFO per producer only; there is deliberately no global order, which removes any temptation for cross-lane coordination.
scenarios.use_case: Ingestion and telemetry lanes where many independent producers stream into a single batch-oriented consumer (log pipelines, metrics fan-in, agent work completion queues) with bounded memory and overload that must drop, never block

invariants: a value offered is received by exactly one partner, or the offering caller is told the exchange failed — never both, never neither
exchanges are symmetric: if A received B's value then B received A's
two callers that are both waiting are eventually paired
a caller released by cancellation or close gets an error and its value is never delivered
scenarios.title: Symmetric pairwise exchange (two parties swap one value each)
scenarios.tradeoffs: There is no buffering and no fan-out: a caller waits until exactly one partner arrives. The design question is whether spreading callers over an arena of meeting slots beats a single lock; the correctness hazard is cancellation racing the match, which must either withdraw the offer or complete the exchange, never both and never neither.
scenarios.use_case: Hand-off points where two goroutines must meet and trade — buffer swapping between a filler and a drainer, pairing a request with a responder, elimination back-off for a contended structure — with cancellation on either side

invariants: a send that returns nil was received (and, where separate, acknowledged) by every member that was joined throughout it
a member that leaves releases a sender waiting on it
a send returns its context's error once the context is done, however many members are stalled
after an abandoned send the next send completes normally: late acknowledgements are not credited to it
members that keep participating observe every completed value, in order
scenarios.title: Barrier broadcast with a sender deadline, mid-broadcast departure and late acknowledgement
scenarios.tradeoffs: As for the lock-step barrier, publisher latency is bounded by the slowest member — until the deadline, after which the value is abandoned and members may or may not have seen it. The implementation has to keep its accounting exact across an abandoned barrier: an acknowledgement that arrives late must not be credited to the next value, and a departing member must release the publisher.
scenarios.use_case: Coordinated reconfiguration and epoch changes where the publisher needs every current member to receive and acknowledge a value, but must be able to give up at a deadline and carry on, and where members may leave at any moment

invariants: within one subscription session, values are never duplicated or reordered
churn never deadlocks, panics or corrupts a publisher
every long-lived session eventually observes the final value (lossless variants) or the latest value (conflating variants)
scenarios.title: Broadcast under ephemeral membership (high subscribe/unsubscribe churn)
scenarios.tradeoffs: Subscribe/unsubscribe cost and its contention with Send dominate; implementations that rebuild or lock the whole registry per membership change degrade, while per-value guarantees may legitimately weaken to 'no corruption, no stall, no duplicate/reordered delivery within a session'.
scenarios.use_case: Short-lived consumer workloads — per-request subscriptions, websocket sessions, plugin hooks — where subscriptions are created and destroyed continuously while publishing proceeds

invariants: correctness invariants of the implementation's own loss policy hold at N=32 in tests (N up to 512 in benchmarks)
Send completes without deadlock at full fan-out
scenarios.title: Broadcast at large fan-out (hundreds of subscribers)
scenarios.tradeoffs: O(N)-rendezvous designs pay linearly per Send; O(1)-wake designs pay in buffering/conflation. The scenario measures that scaling honestly rather than declaring a universal winner.
scenarios.use_case: Fan-out to hundreds of simultaneous consumers for dashboards, game-state replication and notification storms, where per-Send cost scaling with N is the deciding factor

invariants: no consumer ever observes a torn value (all words equal)
values are never duplicated or reordered within a session
scenarios.title: Wide/multi-word payload broadcast integrity
scenarios.tradeoffs: Pointer/slot publication costs an indirection but guarantees atomic observation; direct struct writes into shared slots are faster but can tear or trip the race detector under overrun.
scenarios.use_case: Dissemination of multi-word values (structs, snapshots, frames) for consumers that must never observe a torn, half-published value

invariants: a cancelled subscriber stops promptly and never blocks a publisher afterwards
Close (where it exists) is idempotent
no facet exercises a lifecycle operation the implementation does not document
scenarios.title: Cancellation and close lifecycle
scenarios.tradeoffs: Implementations without a Close/context story are structurally limited here regardless of hot-path merit; facets must only exercise the lifecycle an implementation actually documents.
scenarios.use_case: Long-running services where contexts are cancelled and broadcasters are closed mid-stream, and shutdown must be prompt, idempotent and leak-free

invariants: Publish with zero subscribers never blocks and reports 0 (or the documented equivalent)
a subscriber registered after idle publishes receives subsequent values per the scenario's loss policy
scenarios.title: Zero-subscriber and edge lifecycle
scenarios.tradeoffs: Fast paths for the empty case matter for idle-heavy workloads; several synchronous designs legitimately treat 'no subscribers' specially, which must be verified rather than assumed.
scenarios.use_case: Idle-period publishing and start-up/shut-down edges for any broadcaster: publishing with nobody listening, subscribing after idle periods, double unsubscribe
